name: Maya Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and this is confidential. What does a normal day on your building site look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I fit large timber wall and floor panels on a mid-rise apartment site. I have a vocational trade certificate, and after years of lifting work I still feel each bracket by hand before a crane lets go. A floor appearing between Monday and Friday keeps the job interesting.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Wind stops the crane and the delivery order is sometimes wrong. I use an AI app every day to check panel numbers and translate site notes, then compare its answer with the paper plan. Dev, my partner, and I have two children in school and a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the AI checker still catches a wrong timber panel before the crane turns up. If that is as far as it gets, fine; the crew still has plenty to build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev and I have more than six months saved, both of us earn, and my site rate is good. The mortgage and our two children’s school costs are real, but a plateau would leave our plans intact.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep installing timber panels and running my daily AI drawing check. I would also keep using the phone translator with the crew, but I would check bracket sizes on the printed plans myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, maybe a bit bored. I like a new tool, but I do not need a revolution to pay the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the checker catch last week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A panel number on the delivery sheet did not match the bracket set. I asked the site lead to stop the lift until the warehouse confirmed the right panel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start a new course now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not because of this card. I might study design one day, but right now I have a full crew shift and two children with homework.

say: I would call the existing **panel checker** useful even if wider AI progress stalls.
I would tell the crew **timber panels** still need people checking brackets and lifting safely.
think: Our **two wages** and strong savings keep the mortgage and school costs manageable.
I would feel some **boredom**, not a threat to my current job.
do: Keep fitting **timber panels** and checking bracket sizes on printed plans.
Use the existing **AI drawing checker** and crew translator each workday.
feel: **Calm**, with mild disappointment about limited new tools.
S0.quote: I do not need a revolution to pay the mortgage.
fieldNote: Her daily AI use is **existing practice**, so continuation fits the action.
A second wage, higher site pay, many local jobs and **strong savings** make the plateau secure.

steps.text: Keep fitting timber panels and checking the existing AI drawing output

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the site crew that automated buying could reduce missed panels, but the drawings still have to match the slab. I would ask the union steward for a meeting on who checks AI orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Office purchasing may shrink first, while panel installation stays hands-on. My own job looks safe for now, but if contractors demand faster lifts because plans are instant, paid waiting time and shift lengths could change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn the new AI procurement screen if our contractor grants access, then compare its next two orders with what the crane actually lifts. I would attend the union meeting and ask for a signed site check before orders become final.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about new targets, not afraid of losing our house. I would rather catch one wrong panel than win a race on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the site check cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The panel ID, the lifting bracket and the measured opening. The person signing has to walk the site, not just click a green box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a shorter shift hurt your household?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe if it becomes a pattern, but there is no cut yet. Dev and I would compare several pay packets before changing the family budget.

say: I would ask for a **signed site check** before AI timber orders become final.
I would bring the issue to a **union steward meeting** with the panel crew.
think: My **installation job** looks secure while office buying may shrink.
Faster targets could alter **waiting pay or shifts**, though no cut is certain yet.
do: Learn the new **AI buying screen** if the contractor grants access and compare two orders.
Attend the **union meeting** to seek a signed site check for panels and brackets.
feel: **Anxious** about changing targets while household money remains secure.
S1.quote: The person signing has to walk the site, not just click a green box.
fieldNote: She proposes a specific **human check** on panel IDs and brackets.
New procurement controls are distinct from her **existing drawing checker**, and she needs contractor access.

steps.text: Learn AI buying controls if given access and compare two timber orders
Attend union meeting to request signed panel and bracket checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI in 2028 can redesign the panel order, but a person still guides the crane load. By around 2031 a capable robot might install panels, and I want its wind limits tested on a real site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be forty eight at the robot date and still paying the mortgage. My site hours could shrink then, although our savings, Dev’s wage and nearby building jobs let us make a plan rather than panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my present timber shifts while they pay and ask the contractor for a funded robot-rigging course tied to an actual job. If a paid operator vacancy is posted, I would complete the course and apply; otherwise I would check nearby timber projects before leaving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing hands-on hours, but not overwhelmed. My children need a parent who can pay the bills and come home in one piece.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for an operator course without a vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We could afford the fee. Time away from paid construction shifts costs our household money. I want a posted role and paid training hours before I commit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What wind test would persuade you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A gust strong enough to pause our ordinary crane lift, with the robot stopping as promptly as our banksman. I would want the stop recorded, not edited out of a demonstration.

say: Thinking AI in **2028** changes plans before 2031 robots can install timber panels.
I would require **real wind trials** before a robot guides crane loads on site.
think: My **site hours** could shrink while the mortgage and children’s costs continue.
Dev’s **wage**, savings and local jobs give us time to respond.
do: Keep **timber installation shifts** while the contractor pays them.
Complete a **funded rigging course** only if a paid operator vacancy is posted.
feel: **Anxious** about possible lost hands-on hours, with several practical buffers.
S2.quote: Time away from paid construction shifts costs our household money.
fieldNote: Her course decision needs both a **posted job** and paid training time.
She responds to the robot phase around **2031**, not an invented immediate loss of manual work in 2028.

steps.text: Keep installing timber panels while paid shifts continue
Complete funded robot-rigging training only if a paid operator vacancy is posted

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew five years is enough to test a panel robot in the rain, wind and cramped corners we actually get. An easy warehouse floor proves little about a half-built block.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2031 would speed the drawing side first. Robots reach panel fitting around 2034, when I will be fifty one and still need work; I could build a role checking how the machine meets the structure if paid posts exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would start a technical course in timber inspection next winter if the contractor pays for the course and gives me paid study hours. Until an inspection vacancy is posted, I would keep the panel crew job and ask for the test results.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with a workable runway. Five years gives me a chance to add a skill without betting the mortgage on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you study in the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Moisture, fasteners and how a timber panel takes load. A neat digital model can still hide a wet timber joint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the crew for an unpaid inspection placement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A placement has to pay enough to protect our mortgage and school costs, or I stay on the crew.

say: I would demand **real-site robot trials** before 2034 panel fitting changes crew numbers.
I would learn **timber inspection** if paid study time is provided.
think: I will still need **construction wages** at fifty one when robots arrive.
A new **inspection role** may exist, but I cannot assume a vacancy.
do: Start **timber inspection training** next winter only with funded fees and paid study hours.
Keep **panel crew shifts** until a paid inspection vacancy covers family costs.
feel: **Uneasy** about future job shape, with time to gain a funded skill.
S3.quote: A neat digital model can still hide a wet timber joint.
fieldNote: She commits to actual training, but only with **funded fees** and paid time.
Any job change requires a **paid vacancy** that covers mortgage and school bills.

steps.text: Start timber inspection course next winter only with funded fees and paid study hours
Keep timber panel shifts until an inspection vacancy covers family costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the apprentices to demand real hours on building sites. A decade gives apprentices time to touch timber before a robot lifts it. Thinking AI in 2036 changes drawings first and capable robots follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be fifty six when the robots arrive, still too young to treat retirement as a plan. Dev and I can use our savings and wages to prepare, but both children will have their own choices by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the panel crew and daily drawing checks during 2026. If the contractor offers paid study time, I would complete a timber-inspection course before 2036; in the first year after 2036, I would compare actual site vacancies before changing roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm enough to make a long plan, uneasy for new starters who might not get enough real lifts. The ten years matter if workers help shape the training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you fund the course yourself if the contractor refuses?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might pay a modest fee from savings if Dev and I agree, but not take unpaid months off. A paid study arrangement would make the decision much easier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should apprentices practise now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Reading a panel label, checking the bracket with a hand measure, and stopping a lift when wind rises. Those habits will matter even if a robot does the lifting later.

say: I would press for **hands-on apprenticeship** before 2036 thinking AI and 2039 robots reshape timber construction.
I would tell the crew **wind-stop practice** should stay in training.
think: I expect to need **paid work** beyond the 2039 robot date.
Our **savings and wages** allow planning without assuming the children’s future choices.
do: Keep **2026 panel shifts** and the existing daily drawing checks.
Complete **timber inspection training** before 2036 if paid study time is offered.
feel: **Uneasy** for new starters, while confident my household can prepare.
S4.quote: A decade gives apprentices time to touch timber before a robot lifts it.
fieldNote: She separates **2026 work** from a conditional course before 2036 and vacancy decisions after it.
She leaves **retirement out** of the plan because the robot date falls during her working years.

steps.text: Keep timber panel shifts and existing drawing checks during 2026
Complete timber inspection course before 2036 if paid study time is offered
Compare actual site vacancies after 2036 before changing roles

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable robots could reach timber fitting in 2031 while we still have a mortgage and school bills. Paid training for a posted operator role and honest wind trials would help me act.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks a robot after a bad lift. A machine can lift the panel, but someone still has to answer for the bracket.

headlineQuote: A machine can lift the panel, but someone still has to answer for the bracket.
portrait: **Maya**, 43, fits timber panels with a trade certificate, higher pay, strong savings and many nearby building sites.
She and Dev support **two school-age children** and a mortgage, making paid shifts important despite their financial buffer.
She uses **AI daily**, presses for worker checks and would learn new site skills with funded, paid training.
The **2028 case** worries her because robots could reduce panel-fitting hours around 2031.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could reduce timber fitting shifts after capable robots arrive around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training** for a posted operator role and real wind trials would help her plan.
